frictionVectors.title: EU GAS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: European demand and price volatility remain important to Algeria’s fiscal position. Long-term contracts provide leverage, but export concentration limits strategic flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: SAHEL BORDER PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Instability across Mali, Niger, and Libya increases security costs and complicates Algeria’s non-interventionist regional posture.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE FINANCE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese lending and construction remain embedded in Angola’s transport and energy infrastructure. Debt restructuring has increased Luanda’s room for maneuver but has not removed dependency risks.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS CORRIDOR
frictionVectors.details: US and European backing for the Lobito Corridor is expanding Angola’s strategic importance while intensifying competition over regional copper and cobalt logistics.

frictionVectors.title: NIGER BORDER STANDOFF
frictionVectors.details: Political tensions with Niger have disrupted cross-border commerce and complicated operations linked to the Niger-Benin oil export pipeline.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCY
frictionVectors.details: Cotonou’s role as a regional logistics hub creates exposure to Nigerian trade conditions and external financing for port and corridor infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: DE BEERS NEGOTIATIONS
frictionVectors.details: Botswana is pressing for a larger share of diamond value and greater domestic beneficiation. The dispute tests whether the country can convert bargaining power into durable industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: DIVERSIFICATION GAP
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on diamonds leaves Botswana vulnerable to global demand shifts, while new coal, copper, and critical-mineral projects remain limited in scale.

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY TIES
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou’s expanding security relationship with Russia reduces Western influence but risks creating a new dependency tied to military support and mining access.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD-SECTOR CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: The government is tightening oversight of artisanal and industrial gold production to capture more revenue, but insecurity and informal networks constrain effective state control.

highlights: Gold and nickel ambitions face weak state oversight

frictionVectors.title: MINERAL GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Informal gold exports and opaque licensing reduce public revenue and leave Burundi vulnerable to cross-border trading networks. Nickel development offers leverage but depends heavily on foreign capital and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: REGIONAL SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo constrain trade and security cooperation. Burundi's dependence on external financing narrows its room for sovereign policy choices.

highlights: Tourism and aid create external dependence

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND MARITIME COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and other maritime assets attract European, North American, and wider Atlantic interest. Foreign investment can upgrade infrastructure but may limit national control over strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: ENERGY AND WATER VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago remains exposed to imported fuel, desalination costs, and tourism shocks. Renewable-energy expansion improves resilience but still requires external finance and technology.

highlights: Oil, gas, timber, and minerals remain externally contested
Conflict fragments infrastructure and state authority

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE-ROUTE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues and major transport projects rely on foreign operators, lenders, and export corridors. Chinese-backed infrastructure expands capacity while increasing long-term financial and strategic exposure.

frictionVectors.title: ANGLOPHONE AND FAR-NORTH CONFLICTS
frictionVectors.details: Insurgencies disrupt roads, agriculture, and local resource governance, weakening Yaoundé's control outside core administrative areas. Security cooperation with external partners remains necessary but politically sensitive.

highlights: Mining sovereignty is overshadowed by armed patronage
Russian security backing trades access for influence

frictionVectors.title: RUSSIAN SECURITY-RESOURCE NEXUS
frictionVectors.details: Russian-backed security personnel provide regime protection while gaining political and commercial leverage around gold and diamond activity. Weak transparency prevents the state from capturing reliable public value.

frictionVectors.title: CORRIDOR AND BORDER FRAGMENTATION
frictionVectors.details: Armed groups and porous borders disrupt trade routes linking the country to Cameroon, Chad, Sudan, and the Congo basin. Dependence on external peacekeeping and neighboring corridors limits sovereign infrastructure planning.

highlights: Oil remains the fiscal anchor and strategic vulnerability
Post-French realignment broadens options but raises risk

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND PIPELINE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbon revenues and export infrastructure remain dominated by foreign technical, financial, and marketing partners. Production volatility and opaque revenue management constrain national control over fiscal policy.

frictionVectors.title: SUDAN AND SAHEL SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: War in Sudan and instability across the Sahel generate refugee, arms, and border-security pressures. As traditional Western military ties change, N'Djamena may gain diplomatic flexibility while becoming more dependent on a wider mix of external security actors.

frictionVectors.title: French control and Mayotte dispute
frictionVectors.details: France retains effective control over Mayotte, making territorial sovereignty and migration management the central external-pressure issue for Moroni. The dispute limits bilateral trust while Comoros remains economically dependent on French-linked assistance and remittances.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence in maritime development
frictionVectors.details: Limited state capacity leaves fisheries, port modernization, and prospective offshore resources dependent on foreign finance and technical partners. Competition among Gulf, French, and other investors could expand infrastructure without substantially improving local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict and cross-border mineral networks
frictionVectors.details: The M23 conflict and broader insecurity in the east continue to weaken Kinshasa's control over territory, transport corridors, and mining areas. Regional actors and informal networks remain linked to the movement of coltan, gold, and other minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Unequal strategic-minerals partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain a major position in copper and cobalt, while the United States, European Union, and Gulf actors seek alternative access and supply-chain influence. Contract renegotiation and local-processing ambitions are improving leverage but remain constrained by governance and infrastructure deficits.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State revenues and export capacity remain heavily tied to offshore oil, leaving Brazzaville exposed to price shifts and dependent on foreign operators and service providers. Limited diversification reduces domestic control over the wider resource economy.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction remain important for roads, telecommunications, and energy infrastructure, while French and other Western commercial interests retain influence in hydrocarbons and logistics. Debt obligations and opaque contracting can narrow policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance of cocoa value chains
frictionVectors.details: Cote d'Ivoire has strengthened producer regulation and seeks more domestic processing, but multinational traders and global buyers still capture substantial value and shape market access. Climate stress and farmer-income pressures amplify the sovereignty challenge.

frictionVectors.title: Port and strategic-infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's port expansion and transport corridors attract Chinese, European, Gulf, and other investors, improving national connectivity while creating long-term dependence on external capital and operators. The government retains comparatively strong bargaining capacity within the region.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military-base dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position near the Bab el-Mandeb through a dense concentration of French, US, Chinese, Japanese, and other military facilities. This generates revenue and deterrence but makes national security and foreign-policy room highly dependent on external powers.

frictionVectors.title: Port debt and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed port and rail investments, alongside competition from Gulf-linked and regional logistics interests, have increased infrastructure capacity but added financial and operational dependencies. Ethiopia's reliance on Djiboutian corridors strengthens leverage while concentrating exposure to regional instability.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and strategic assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and IMF-linked reforms are encouraging asset sales and expanded Gulf investment in ports, logistics, and real estate. This brings liquidity but can dilute Cairo's long-term control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Nile water security
frictionVectors.details: The unresolved GERD dispute with Ethiopia remains Egypt's central resource-security concern. Cairo retains diplomatic and military leverage, but has not secured binding guarantees over downstream flows.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining oil and gas output leaves the state dependent on foreign operators, technical expertise, and export markets. Production-sharing arrangements provide revenue but limit domestic control over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and port infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Punta Europa complex and associated maritime infrastructure remain vulnerable to external capital and regional competition. Malabo is attempting to turn them into a gas-processing hub, but financing and feedstock access are constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline gives it strategic value amid competition involving Gulf states, Türkiye, Egypt, and other regional actors. Asmara seeks to monetize access while resisting permanent dependence on any outside power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining exposure
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide hard currency but rely heavily on foreign capital, equipment, and expertise. Sanctions risk, labor-rights criticism, and opaque governance complicate efforts to maximize national resource capture.

frictionVectors.title: Customs-union exposure
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini's fiscal position is tightly tied to Southern African Customs Union receipts, leaving sovereignty vulnerable to regional trade and policy shifts. South Africa remains the dominant economic and logistical counterweight.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and industrial concessions
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, and export manufacturing depend on external markets, investors, and infrastructure corridors. These sectors generate employment but constrain domestic control over land use, value chains, and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam has increased Addis Ababa's leverage over regional energy and water diplomacy. It continues to face intense opposition from Egypt and Sudan, with no comprehensive operating agreement.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, foreign-exchange shortages, and reliance on external port corridors limit Ethiopia's autonomy despite its large domestic market. Competition over access through Djibouti, Somaliland, and Eritrea has become a core strategic issue.

highlights: Military transition tightens control over oil and mining
Gabon seeks greater local value from manganese and timber

frictionVectors.title: Resource Nationalism Versus Investor Confidence
frictionVectors.details: Transitional authorities are pressing for stronger state participation and local processing in oil, manganese, and timber. Renegotiation risks could unsettle established foreign operators and delay investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Rail Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export capacity remains concentrated around foreign-linked port, rail, and mining infrastructure. Control of the Transgabonese corridor is central to whether resource rents translate into broader sovereign leverage.

highlights: Small-state sovereignty remains tied to external financing
Senegalese trade and security links dominate strategic space

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-Dependent Connectivity
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for surrounding transport access, market connectivity, and aspects of security cooperation. This provides practical stability but limits independent control over regional infrastructure choices.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew and Groundnut Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Agricultural exports remain vulnerable to foreign traders, price swings, and limited domestic processing. The resulting value leakage constrains fiscal sovereignty and rural bargaining power.

highlights: Debt pressure narrows room for resource-led development
Gold, oil, and emerging lithium assets face stronger scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Mining Revenue and Local Processing
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital remains important in gold and prospective lithium development, while Ghana seeks more refining, local procurement, and fiscal capture. Illegal mining and environmental damage further weaken state control over mineral rents.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and Creditor Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and international financial support constrain policy flexibility, including subsidies and infrastructure spending. Fiscal stabilization can improve credibility while reducing the government's room to pursue resource-nationalist policies.

highlights: Bauxite expansion strengthens state bargaining power
Simandou infrastructure could reorder Guinea's economy

frictionVectors.title: Simandou Corridor Competition
frictionVectors.details: The railway, port, and mining complex is attracting major foreign investment and could transform export capacity. Its scale creates leverage for the junta but also risks locking Guinea into externally controlled infrastructure and commodity chains.

frictionVectors.title: Junta Legitimacy and Mining Governance
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are using contract reviews and local-content demands to increase state control over bauxite and iron ore. Political uncertainty and limited transparency raise risks of abrupt concessions, elite capture, and investor backlash.

highlights: Cashew exports remain the central economic lifeline
Political fragility leaves ports and trade routes exposed

frictionVectors.title: Cashew Trader Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers and regional intermediaries capture much of the value from the cashew economy, while domestic processing remains limited. Seasonal export dependence leaves the state vulnerable to price manipulation and liquidity shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Port, Security, and Illicit Networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and recurring political tensions make Bissau's port and coastal routes vulnerable to external commercial and illicit influence. Limited maritime enforcement reduces sovereign control over fisheries, customs revenue, and trafficking risks.

highlights: Port and mineral sovereignty under scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Strategic Assets
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and reliance on multilateral and bilateral lenders constrain Nairobi's fiscal and infrastructure choices. The Mombasa port corridor remains strategically important to foreign financiers and regional trade partners.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is seeking greater domestic value addition in minerals and energy, but foreign capital and technology remain influential in exploration and project development.

highlights: Water exports deepen dependence on South Africa
Textile and infrastructure sectors remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Water transfers to South Africa provide vital revenue but leave Lesotho dependent on Pretoria for project financing, implementation, and market access. Delays and governance disputes can directly affect national income.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The textile sector depends heavily on external buyers and trade preferences, while infrastructure investment remains linked to South African and international financing.

highlights: Infrastructure recovery relies on foreign capital

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large mining operators retain substantial influence over transport, energy, and export infrastructure. Liberia's challenge is converting concession activity into durable domestic processing, jobs, and public revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Corridor Financing
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, and power projects depend on foreign investors and donors, limiting Monrovia's room to impose stronger local-content and sovereign-control conditions.

highlights: Oil revenues remain divided by rival authorities
Foreign security patrons shape energy access

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and security centers can disrupt production, export terminals, and budget transfers despite the formal role of the National Oil Corporation. Hydrocarbon control remains the central lever of domestic power.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Energy Influence
frictionVectors.details: Turkish, Russian, Egyptian, Emirati, and European interests continue to affect security arrangements and energy diplomacy. External backing raises the risk that infrastructure access will be traded for political or military concessions.

highlights: Mining enclaves outpace domestic value creation
Critical minerals attract competing foreign interests

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining Chains
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are largely financed and operated through foreign-linked consortia. Madagascar remains exposed to commodity-price swings while local processing and fiscal capture lag behind exports.

frictionVectors.title: Land, Logistics, and Political Risk
frictionVectors.details: Mining corridors and port infrastructure can generate conflict over land, environmental damage, and revenue sharing. Political uncertainty makes long-term concessions vulnerable to renegotiation and external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: IMF and creditor conditions strongly influence fiscal, energy, and infrastructure policy. Debt restructuring limits Lilongwe's room to negotiate resource deals from a position of strength.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in uranium, rare earths, and other minerals is increasing, but regulatory capacity and local value-add remain limited.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Footprint
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of French and UN forces has been followed by deeper reliance on Russian-linked security personnel and regional partnerships, increasing sovereignty risks and operational opacity.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Nationalism Versus Capacity
frictionVectors.details: Bamako is seeking larger state revenues and ownership stakes in gold projects, but confrontations with international operators could reduce investment and technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The shared offshore gas project with Senegal can improve state revenues, but dependence on foreign operators, export infrastructure, and bilateral coordination constrains national control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Port Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore exports remain tied to foreign capital and the Nouadhibou rail-port corridor, leaving the economy exposed to commodity prices and infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos and Diego Garcia Settlement
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is pressing its sovereignty claim while the future of the Diego Garcia military facility remains strategically sensitive to the United Kingdom, United States, and regional powers.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital in Port Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Expansion of maritime and logistics capacity depends on foreign finance and partnerships, creating long-term leverage concerns despite strong domestic institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco continues linking phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy, and infrastructure projects to its sovereignty claim, drawing legal and diplomatic challenges from Algeria and the Polisario Front.

frictionVectors.title: External Dependence in Mega-Projects
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and other foreign partners provide capital and technology for ports, rail, renewables, and green hydrogen, creating competition for influence around strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence continues to threaten northern gas infrastructure and raises Mozambique's dependence on foreign military and private-security support.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Projects
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies retain major influence over liquefied natural gas development, limiting near-term domestic control over strategic gas revenues.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Strategic Projects
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and investors dominate financing and technology for uranium, green hydrogen, and offshore oil projects, creating sovereignty risks despite strong state regulation.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Export Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Namibia relies heavily on regional corridors and foreign-linked logistics investment to export minerals and future energy products.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Oil Renegotiations
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is seeking greater control over uranium and petroleum assets, increasing tensions with established foreign operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Border Closures
frictionVectors.details: Regional isolation and disrupted trade routes constrain access to fuel, equipment, and export markets, weakening the state's ability to convert resource control into revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Multinational Oil Leverage
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies remain central to production, financing, and technical capacity, while subsidy reform and contract disputes complicate efforts to increase Nigerian control.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline Theft and Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Vandalism, crude theft, and insecurity in the Niger Delta reduce public revenue and preserve dependence on external operators and security providers.

frictionVectors.title: Conflict-Mineral Allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's role in regional mineral supply chains and alleged support for armed actors in eastern Congo generate sustained diplomatic and commercial pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Aid and Investment Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Strong domestic administrative control is offset by reliance on external aid, concessional finance, and foreign investment for infrastructure and strategic sectors.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe retains formal control over its offshore blocks, but limited technical and financial capacity leaves exploration dependent on foreign operators and changing licensing partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal Fishing Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime surveillance exposes the country’s waters to illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing, reducing the value of its fisheries and limiting effective control over its exclusive economic zone.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Contract Reset
frictionVectors.details: New production from Sangomar and the Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major fiscal upside, but efforts to increase state participation and local content risk friction with foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Industrial Fishing Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets and declining fish stocks are generating pressure from coastal communities, while enforcement and licensing reforms remain central to protecting Senegalese access to marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Tuna Access
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from licensing revenue and tuna-related infrastructure, but dependence on foreign fleets creates recurring concerns over resource depletion, transparency, and equitable value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Strategic Competition
frictionVectors.details: The country’s ports, maritime domain, and communications links attract interest from India, China, and other partners, requiring careful balancing to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Large-Scale Mining Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain dominated by foreign capital and export logistics, leaving Sierra Leone exposed to commodity cycles and persistent disputes over taxation, land, and environmental impacts.

frictionVectors.title: Coastal Fisheries Enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Illegal and unreported fishing, including activity linked to foreign industrial fleets, undermines artisanal communities and highlights gaps in patrol capacity and licensing oversight.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Energy Security
frictionVectors.details: Offshore petroleum cooperation with Turkey and other external partners could expand state revenue, but weak institutions and contested federal authority create risks of opaque contracts and uneven benefit distribution.

frictionVectors.title: Somaliland–Ethiopia Corridor Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Competing claims over ports, maritime access, and recognition in Somaliland draw in Ethiopia, Türkiye, Gulf states, and Western partners, complicating Somalia’s control of its coastline and offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: South Africa is balancing investment and processing demands from China, the United States, and the European Union while seeking greater domestic beneficiation. Policy uncertainty and infrastructure constraints limit bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Eskom and logistics constraints
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and freight-rail and port weaknesses continue to reduce export capacity and national control over mineral value chains. Private-sector participation is expanding but raises concerns over strategic asset governance.

highlights: Oil lifeline exposed to Sudan war

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline dependence through Sudan
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan relies on infrastructure and transit routes controlled beyond its borders, leaving oil revenues vulnerable to conflict, sabotage, and bargaining by Sudanese authorities and armed actors.

frictionVectors.title: External competition around oil and security
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and regional firms retain major influence in petroleum operations, while neighboring states and Gulf-linked networks shape security and trade access. Weak institutions limit transparent control of resource revenues.

highlights: War fragments the national resource base
Gold and ports draw external rivalry

frictionVectors.title: Gold war economy
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival military networks, with regional and Gulf-linked actors competing for access. The conflict has sharply reduced civilian oversight of mining and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and associated logistics corridors are strategically important to outside powers seeking naval, commercial, and mineral access. War conditions make infrastructure vulnerable to coercion and foreign influence.

highlights: Ports and corridors become strategic assets

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Dar es Salaam and planned or expanding transport corridors attract Gulf, Chinese, and other foreign capital. The government is pursuing commercial expansion while facing pressure to preserve regulatory control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and gas bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking more local value addition and stronger fiscal terms in gold, critical minerals, and prospective LNG. Delays and regulatory disputes reflect an effort to rebalance foreign investment against national ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Port dependency and foreign capital
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé is a key transshipment and supply hub for inland West Africa, attracting sustained foreign commercial influence. Concentration of logistics capacity creates both revenue opportunities and sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and instability from Burkina Faso threaten northern transport routes and state access. External security assistance and regional intelligence cooperation are increasingly important to protecting trade infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing conditionality
frictionVectors.details: European funding and political engagement remain tied to Tunisia's role in limiting irregular migration, creating external leverage over domestic policy. Financial stress and limited alternatives weaken Tunisian bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Energy import vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on imported hydrocarbons and electricity exposes Tunisia to supply and price pressure. Renewable investment is growing, but foreign capital and technology remain important to scaling domestic capacity.

highlights: Oil development advances under foreign partners

frictionVectors.title: Lake Albert oil and export pipeline
frictionVectors.details: Uganda's oil project depends on Chinese financing and the Tanzania-linked East African Crude Oil Pipeline, leaving timelines and revenues exposed to external partners, sanctions pressure, and environmental opposition.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese infrastructure and debt exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects improve connectivity but increase dependence on external contractors and financing. Strategic infrastructure is therefore expanding without fully strengthening domestic ownership.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of copper value chains
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater local processing, fiscal returns, and state influence over copper and critical-mineral projects, while international mining firms retain major capital and technical leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and infrastructure conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms have stabilized access to external finance but constrain fiscal choices. Chinese, Western, and multilateral actors continue competing for influence over strategic infrastructure and mining.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and platinum externalization
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors, particularly Chinese firms, dominate important mineral capital and processing networks, while Zimbabwe struggles to convert resource extraction into broad domestic industrial gains.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and alternative financing
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted market access push Harare toward Chinese, Russian, and regional channels for investment and trade. This reduces dependence on Western finance but can increase opacity and bargaining asymmetry.
